content: Harvest mites, also known as chiggers, are tiny arachnids belonging to the family Trombiculidae. These mites are nearly microscopic, measuring approximately 0.4 mm in size, and are characterized by their chrome-orange coloration. In their larval stage, they are parasitic and attach to various animals, including humans, to feed on skin cells. Unlike ticks, they do not consume blood. Instead, they inject digestive enzymes into the skin, breaking down skin cells into a liquid form that they consume. This process causes significant irritation, swelling, and intense itching. The affected areas often develop red, pimple-like bumps (papules), hives, or rashes, particularly in sun-exposed regions of the body. Itching typically begins after the larvae detach from the skin. The larvae are six-legged and inhabit environments such as berry patches, tall grass, weeds, woodland edges, pine straw, leaves, and tree bark. They are commonly found in areas frequented by their hosts, such as rodents. After feeding, the larvae drop to the ground, where they transition into nymphs and eventually mature into eight-legged adults. Adult harvest mites are not parasitic and feed on plant material. Female mites lay 3-8 eggs on leaves or under plant roots before dying in the autumn. Harvest mites are prevalent in many parts of the world, particularly in hot and humid regions. In Europe and North America, they are most active during the summer months. In the United States, they are commonly found in the southeast, south, and midwest, but are rare or absent in far northern areas, high mountains, and deserts. In East Asia and the South Pacific, harvest mites are significant vectors of scrub typhus, a disease caused by the parasite Orientia tsutsugamushi. The mites acquire the parasite from infected rodent hosts and pass it to their offspring. Scrub typhus symptoms in humans include fever, headache, muscle pain, cough, and gastrointestinal issues. In North America, heavy infestations of harvest mites can cause severe symptoms in children, such as fever, fatigue, and a hallucinatory sensation of floating outside the body. Contrary to popular myths, harvest mite larvae do not burrow into the skin. Instead, they pierce the skin and inject enzymes to digest cellular contents. Another misconception is that applying rubbing alcohol can kill the mites or alleviate symptoms; this method only causes additional pain and discomfort. Special attention should be given to areas such as the ankles, feet, behind the knees, underarms, and chest. An Epsom salt bath or wading in saltwater can help alleviate itching. Another method involves using adhesive tape to remove the mites from the skin. However, once symptoms appear, it may be too late to prevent further irritation. Scratching the affected areas should be avoided, as it can worsen irritation and increase the risk of secondary infection. Topical treatments such as calamine lotion, petroleum jelly, or baby oil can help reduce itching. Clear nail polish is sometimes applied to the bites to dry out the sores, but this method is based on the misconception that the mites remain embedded in the skin. Antihistamines or corticosteroid creams may be prescribed by a physician to manage symptoms. To prevent chigger bites, individuals should wear protective clothing, such as long pants and tightly woven fabrics, and apply insect repellents containing DEET, catnip oil extract, citronella, or eucalyptus oil. DEET has been shown to be more effective than citrus oil in repelling chiggers. Dusting sulfur on shoes, socks, and pant legs can also be an effective deterrent.
